theory.title: HTTP Redirects: Following the Trail
theory.recap: HTTP responses have status codes: 200 means success. But the 3xx range means something different - the resource has moved, and the client must make a new request to a different URL. Redirects are normal and intentional, but redirect chains must terminate.
theory.plainObjective: Follow the HTTP redirect chain from the first server (302 temporary) to the second (301 permanent HTTPS upgrade) to reach the final HTTPS destination.
theory.summary: Every time you type http:// in a browser and land on https://, a 301 redirect happened. The server told your browser: this resource permanently lives at a different URL. Browsers follow the chain automatically - but developers must design chains that terminate.

bodyParagraphs.heading: 301 Permanent vs 302 Temporary
bodyParagraphs.text: 301 Moved Permanently tells browsers to update their bookmarks and never visit the old URL again. Browsers cache 301s aggressively. 302 Found (temporary) says 'the resource is temporarily elsewhere' - browsers check the original URL again next time.

bodyParagraphs.heading: HTTP to HTTPS redirect
bodyParagraphs.text: Sites that want to enforce HTTPS typically have their HTTP server (port 80) respond with 301 to the same path but with https://. This is the HTTPS upgrade redirect. Done correctly, it happens once and browsers cache it.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Redirect loops
bodyParagraphs.text: A redirect loop happens when server A redirects to B, and B redirects back to A (or a longer cycle). Browsers detect this after a few redirects and show an error. Well-designed redirect chains always terminate at a real resource.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Too many redirects
bodyParagraphs.text: Each redirect in a chain is an extra round trip: client → server → redirect → client → new server. Long chains add latency. Google's guidance: keep redirect chains to one or two hops maximum. Each additional redirect adds at least 100ms on a fast connection.

theory.mission:
Your packet starts on port 80, destined for 10.50.3.5.

The first server sends a 302 temporary redirect - follow it. The second server sends a 301 permanent redirect to HTTPS. One path leads to a redirect loop - avoid it. Reach the final HTTPS server.

termIntroductions.headline: HTTP Redirects
termIntroductions.body: A 3xx response tells the client to make a new request to a different URL. The Location header says where. 302 Found = temporary, check back next time. 301 Moved Permanently = update your bookmarks, this URL is gone forever. Browsers follow these automatically.

termIntroductions.headline: 302 Found (Temporary)
termIntroductions.body: This server temporarily redirects your request. It responds: HTTP/1.1 302 Found, Location: /new-path. Your client follows the Location header. Because it is temporary, browsers will check the original URL again next visit - no caching of the redirect.

termIntroductions.headline: Redirect Loop
termIntroductions.body: This path redirects back to the previous server, which redirects here again - infinite loop. Browsers detect this and stop after 10-20 redirects with 'Too many redirects'. This is a server misconfiguration. Go back and follow the chain forward.

termIntroductions.headline: 301 Moved Permanently
termIntroductions.body: This server permanently upgrades you to HTTPS: HTTP/1.1 301, Location: https://... Browsers cache this redirect, so next time they go straight to HTTPS without hitting port 80 at all. One path leads to a broken redirect - the other continues to the HTTPS server.

termIntroductions.headline: Broken Redirect
termIntroductions.body: This redirect points to a domain that doesn't exist or has a misconfigured DNS entry. The browser follows the Location header and gets no response. Go back and take the working HTTPS path.
